idiom_name: one state-owning actor object + bounded mailbox + stable address
implementation_notes: Language-neutral structure: give each entity a single actor object that owns its state privately and is never handed out; communicate by immutable messages sent to a stable address (reference, pid, channel). Buffer incoming messages in a bounded mailbox with an explicit overflow policy and process them strictly one at a time; run a dispatcher or scheduler over the actors so the number of OS threads stays small, and let a supervisor own creation, failure and restart. What changes per language is only which primitive supplies the mailbox and the scheduling - channels, blocking queues, or mailboxes managed by an actor runtime. The classic full structure is justified whenever callers must address entities that outlive a single call and mutate concurrently; if there is one consumer and no state, a plain queue is enough.
code_sketch:
actor = { state, mailbox: bounded queue, address }

send(address, message)                      # never touches state directly

loop:
    msg = mailbox.receive()                # exactly one at a time
    state = handle(state, msg)             # single writer, no locks
    emit replies as messages to other addresses
pitfalls: Letting callers hold the actor object or its state instead of an address reintroduces shared mutable state.
A mailbox without a bound and without an overflow policy turns overload into memory growth.
Assuming guaranteed delivery or global ordering: the pattern provides neither.
Circular wait through ask pattern: actor A asks B while B simultaneously asks A — a deadlock that appears only under concurrent load; avoid by using tell with forward or dedicated aggregator actors.
Restart storm: a supervisor with no restart intensity limits or overly broad strategy (one_for_all) lets one crashing actor terminate its entire subtree.
Location transparency illusion: assuming in-process message semantics when an actor is actually remote; network failures, latency spikes and partial availability require different handling.
Reentrant handlers (await inside handler): suspending a handler mid-processing can interleave messages and invalidate invariants checked before the suspension point.

Wrong move: perform blocking I/O or a long CPU loop inside a handler -> how it fails: the dispatcher or event loop is occupied, so unrelated actors queue behind it and latency spikes -> instead: offload the operation to a dedicated dispatcher or pool and send its result back with a timeout.

Wrong move: leave a mailbox unbounded or let every sender enqueue without admission control -> how it fails: retained payloads and growing latency hide overload until garbage collection and memory exhaustion take down the node -> instead: bound the mailbox and choose reject/backpressure/drop with depth and drop metrics.

Wrong move: supervise only actor creation and ignore restart semantics -> how it fails: crashes lose in-memory state or restart storms repeat side effects and terminate siblings -> instead: choose restart/stop/escalate scope and intensity, persist required state, and make external effects idempotent.

Wrong move: spawn an actor for stateless one-shot work (a fetch, a transform, a fire-and-forget job) -> how it fails: the mailbox serializes what a plain async call would run concurrently and every call needs a bespoke message type - indirection with no shared state to protect -> instead: reserve actors for long-lived stateful ownership and use futures, tasks or plain functions for one-shot computation.

Wrong move: use actor pools as a concurrency throttle or flow-control mechanism instead of state owners -> how it fails: mailboxes become hand-rolled semaphores - throughput drops behind the router, backpressure is invisible and the pool needs retuning whenever load shifts -> instead: express fan-out with futures or structured tasks and keep an actor only where mutable state needs a single writer.

Wrong move: route all inter-component interaction through bespoke actor message protocols -> how it fails: actor protocols do not compose - receivers are hard to substitute, one-off message vocabularies proliferate per boundary and small reusable parts cannot be assembled -> instead: give each actor a narrow published protocol and expose ordinary async functions at the composition boundary.
